title: Garfield County CO well depth and costs
meta_description: Garfield County wells have a 102 ft median depth and 15 gpm median yield. Learn what that means for drilling cost, water levels, and buying land.
h1: Water wells in Garfield County, Colorado
intro_html:
If you’re looking at land or a home on a well anywhere in Garfield County, the state’s well records give a decent picture of what to expect. The county has 12,083 permitted wells on the books, with thousands reporting depth, yield, and water level.

Below is a plain‑language rundown of typical well depths, common production, what drilling usually costs in this geology, and the main risks I’d look at before closing on a property from Parachute and Rifle over to Glenwood Springs and Carbondale.

sections.heading: How deep are Garfield County wells, really
sections.html:
Across Garfield County, reported wells have a median total depth of 102 feet. The middle half run from about 53 to 190 feet, and only about 1% go beyond 600 feet. The deepest well on record is 3,190 feet, but that’s an outlier, not a planning number.

Roughly 47% of wells are under 100 feet and another 43% fall between 100 and 300 feet. That mix tells you most bids will be based on a shallow to moderate hole, but you still need to plan for the upper end of the local range. The county is mostly unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, with some alluvial and Williams Fork work, so depth can jump quickly between a place like Rifle and a spot up a side valley.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you’re likely to get
sections.html:
Production in Garfield County is generally favorable. The median reported pump yield is 15 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells come in between 10 and 15 gpm. That’s strong for an exempt household well and usually more than enough for domestic use plus some outside watering, within permit limits.

Only about 1% of wells report under 1 gpm and 9% are in the 1–5 gpm range. About 31% land between 5 and 15 gpm, and 59% are 15 gpm or higher. So the odds of a true “trickle” well are low, but not zero. In fractured bedrock, two neighboring wells can behave very differently, so always review nearby well logs around places like New Castle or Battlement Mesa before assuming you’ll match the county median.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend in the county
sections.html:
Static water levels, where reported, are fairly shallow. The overall median depth to water is 38 feet, with the middle half between about 19 and 75 feet. That means most pumps aren’t set extremely deep, which helps with equipment sizing and power costs.

Looking by decade, median water levels have bounced around rather than showing a straight decline: about 30 feet in the 1960s, 44 in the 1970s, 53 in the 1980s, then back to roughly the 30s in the 1990s and 2000s, and the upper 30s in the 2010s and 2020s. That suggests local variability tied to where and when wells were drilled, but not a clear countywide crash in the water table. Still, check recent measurements near specific areas like Glenwood Springs or Parachute to be sure your spot isn’t trending worse than the county picture.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and how active permits are
sections.html:
Garfield County has a long drilling history. Permits start in the 1950s and ramp up sharply after that: 19 in the 1950s, 271 in the 1960s, 853 in the 1970s, and 1,405 in the 1980s. Activity peaks in the 1990s with 2,951 permits and stays strong in the 2000s at 2,500. The 2010s still see 1,543, and there are already 852 in the 2020s with records current through 2026.

Most wells are for domestic or household use at about 58%, with stock, irrigation, and a large block of monitoring wells making up the rest. On the drilling side, Shelton Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Wayne) shows the most wells in the records, followed by Authorized (Pe, Pg) and Collins Drilling Co. That density of existing wells around places like Silt and Carbondale gives you plenty of nearby logs to compare before you permit a new one.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Garfield County
sections.html:
In Garfield County’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, typical drilling runs about $50–$75 per foot. At the county’s 102-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole itself in the ballpark of $5,100–$7,600. A complete, turn-key domestic setup with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually falls around $11,100–$19,600 at that depth.

Because the middle half of wells run from about 53 to 190 feet, it’s smart to budget toward the deeper side of that range, especially in fractured bedrock areas. Domestic-only permits have a pumping limit, so higher yield doesn’t change your legal withdrawal, but it can affect pump sizing. Always get a written bid that spells out footage rates, steel or PVC casing, grout, test pumping, and any extras for work in areas like Cattle Creek or Catherine.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
Even with a 15 gpm median yield, about 10% of wells fall at 5 gpm or below, so low-production wells do exist. In fractured-bedrock zones, dry or marginal holes tend to cluster along certain ridges or benches. Reviewing logs from nearby wells is your best defense before you pick a drill site.

On the water quality side, there are mapped concerns: around 691 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 74 historic mine features, and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles across the county. That doesn’t mean your well is bad, but it does mean you should test. Finally, leave room to separate the well from septic tanks and leach fields, and think ahead about where a house, driveway, and future outbuildings will sit so you don’t paint yourself into a corner.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot with a well in Garfield County
sections.html:
For an existing well, pull the Colorado DWR permit and driller’s log and compare the reported depth, yield, and static level to the county medians of 102 feet, 15 gpm, and 38 feet. If the well is much deeper with lower yield than typical for nearby places like Rifle or Mulford, budget for a conservative water-use plan or potential upgrades.

For vacant land, I’d line up three things before closing: a conversation with a local driller using nearby logs, a realistic cost range based on the 53–190 foot middle-depth band, and lab testing on any existing well to check for PFAS, metals, and bacteria. In over-appropriated basins you may be pushed toward augmentation plans; in any case, build your house, septic, and driveway layout around proper well setbacks and future service access.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Garfield County, Colorado?
faq.a: Across Garfield County, reported wells have a median depth of about 102 feet. The middle half fall between roughly 53 and 190 feet, and only about 1% go deeper than 600 feet. Around 47% of wells are under 100 feet and 43% are between 100 and 300 feet. When planning a new well, I’d budget toward the upper end of that local 53–190 foot band.

faq.q: How much water do Garfield County wells usually produce?
faq.a: Production here is generally strong. The median reported pump yield is 15 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells land between 10 and 15 gpm. Only about 1% report under 1 gpm, and 9% fall in the 1–5 gpm range. Roughly 31% are 5–15 gpm and 59% are 15 gpm or more, which is plenty for a typical domestic well under Colorado’s household-use rules.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Garfield County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Garfield County’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, typical drilling prices run about $50–$75 per foot. At the county’s 102-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole alone in the range of about $5,100–$7,600. A complete domestic system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals around $11,100–$19,600 at that depth. Deeper wells toward the 190-foot range will push costs higher.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Garfield County, Colorado?
faq.a: The records don’t give countywide pass/fail answers on water quality, but they do show potential risks. There are about 691 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 74 historic mine features, and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped within roughly 10 miles. That doesn’t automatically mean a problem at your well, but it’s a strong reason to run lab tests for PFAS, metals, and bacteria before relying on it for drinking.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Garfield County wells?
faq.a: Based on reported static water levels, there isn’t a simple steady decline countywide. The median depth to water is about 38 feet overall, with the middle half from roughly 19 to 75 feet. By decade, medians have bounced from around 30 feet in the 1960s, to deeper in the 1970s–1980s, then back into the 30s and upper 30s more recently. Individual areas can differ, so always check recent nearby measurements.
